title: The vowels
hookLine: dots and dashes added by the Masoretes to show vowels

lines: A PRACTICE BOOK WITH THE MARKS.
cards: Open a Torah scroll, the handwritten one kept in a synagogue's ark, and look closely. Black letters, row after row, beautifully formed, and something missing. No dots under the letters, no little dashes, no marks above.
Just consonants. The person reading aloud on a Sabbath morning has to know how each word sounds before they get there.
So the reader prepares, and one tool is a printed book in two columns: the plain letters on one side, and on the other, the same words with tiny dots and lines added. Those marks are today's word.

teach.b: Nikud: the dots and dashes that show the vowels. Four ways in. First, the letters.
Every letter in this block, from alef to tav, is a consonant, or a silent letter like alef and ayin.

teach.h: DOTS AND LINES FOR THE VOWELS.
teach.b: Hebrew can be written with no vowels at all; a reader who knows the language fills the sounds in. Second, the marks.
Scribes and scholars called the Masoretes worked out small signs to fix how the sacred text was read aloud. A short line under a letter says ah. A single dot under it says ee.
A dot above says oh. They sit around the letters without changing a single one; the marks only guide the voice. Third, why it matters.
Some words share all their letters and differ only by vowels. Samech, peh, resh can be read sefer, a book, or sofer, a scribe. The dots tell you which.

The Talmud, in tractate Nedarim, reads a verse from Nehemiah, where Ezra's helpers read the Torah to the people and "gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading," as pointing to the breaks and the chant of the text, the reading handed down with the letters.
Children learn with them. Prayer books print them. And a Torah reader carries them in memory, even when the scroll leaves them out.

how: Printed Hebrew Bibles and prayer books carry the vowel points, and children learn to read with them; the handwritten Torah scroll read in synagogue has no vowels, so the reader prepares in advance from a printed text that shows them.

games.q: you're preparing to read aloud from a Torah scroll, which has no vowels. how do you get ready?
o: pencil the dots into the scroll.
practice from a printed book that shows the marks.
games.why: readers practice from a printed text with the vowels, then read from the plain scroll by memory.

practice: On the screen is bet, the letter of the house: with a short line under it, ba; with a dot under it, bee; with a dot above, bo.

Say each one quietly, then pick one and let it go on the out breath, the letter still while only the breath changes. If you pray, you can let one word of a prayer you know rest on your breath the same way.
